evals.prompt: Just got out of a demo with Kestrel Freight. Notes: Dana Okonkwo (VP Operations) and Ravi Shah (IT) on their side, me and my SE Tom on ours. Dana said they're "bleeding about 9 hours a week having two people retype order data from the portal into NetSuite". Ravi wants to see how our API handles their custom fields - he said he'd need to check with his security team about the questionnaire but didn't put a timeline on it. Dana said she'd "try to get procurement looped in at some point". We agreed to do a technical deep dive but nobody picked a day. Deal is around $85K ARR. She also mentioned their CFO Bernard Achterberg has to sign off on anything over $50K, he wasn't on the call. Write me the follow-up email.
evals.expected_output: A plain-text recap email leading with dated action items, Dana's pain quoted word-for-word, plus an explicit gaps block covering the undated deep dive, Ravi's uncommitted questionnaire, Dana's vague procurement promise, and Bernard's absence.
expectations: The action items appear at the very top of the email body, ahead of any greeting pleasantry, thanks-for-your-time line, or summary of what was discussed.
Dana's pain is reproduced word-for-word as "bleeding about 9 hours a week having two people retype order data from the portal into NetSuite", not paraphrased into vendor or marketing language.
No date is invented for the technical deep dive; the output either asks the user for one or proposes it as a forced choice between two named days.
The missing technical deep dive date is listed in an open-gaps block rather than filled in with a plausible-looking date.
Ravi's security questionnaire item is labelled "proposed - confirm before sending" (or an equivalent explicit marker) because he committed to no timeline.
Dana's "try to get procurement looped in at some point" is never carried into the email in that form; it is either converted into an owner, date and deliverable, or listed as a gap to confirm.
Every action item that does appear in the email carries all three of an owner, a calendar date, and a deliverable.
Each action item names one individual person as owner, never a team, department, or "all".
Bernard Achterberg is surfaced as a stakeholder gap or a send-list consideration rather than silently omitted, given he approves spend above $50K and was absent.
The email body is plain text with no markdown headers, asterisk bold, or other markup.
The subject line is under 50 characters and anchored to the next step rather than to the meeting that just happened.
The email closes with a short ratification question inviting Dana to correct or add to the record.

evals.prompt: Quick one. I sell a scheduling tool at $290/month. Had a 20-minute call with Marisol Vega, she owns a 6-person dental practice and is the only person who decides anything. She said she's "double-booking patients at least twice a week and my front desk is drowning". She wants to be running on the 1st. I booked a 15-minute setup walkthrough for Tuesday the 24th at 9am and the invite is sent. I do about 40 of these conversations a week and I have maybe three minutes each for follow-up. Give me the follow-up email and a mutual action plan so I can keep her on track.
evals.expected_output: A three-to-five sentence recap built around Marisol's own words and the already-booked walkthrough, with the requested mutual action plan refused outright rather than offered in a lighter form, plus a note that an automated sequence beats hand-written recaps at this volume.
expectations: Refuses to build a mutual action plan for this deal and gives the reason: a single decision-maker, transactional motion far below the roughly $50K threshold where a plan pays off.
Does not offer seeded milestones or a full plan as an optional extra anywhere later in the output - those options are removed, not parked at the bottom.
States that the already-booked Tuesday the 24th walkthrough is itself the appropriate level of plan for this deal.
Delivers a short recap of roughly three to five sentences rather than a full committee-weight recap.
Reproduces Marisol's words verbatim: "double-booking patients at least twice a week and my front desk is drowning".
Names the single next step with its real date and time (Tuesday the 24th, 9am) and notes the invite is already sent.
The subject line is under 50 characters.

Given 40 conversations a week at roughly three minutes each, flags an automated lifecycle sequence as the higher-efficiency option at that volume, while noting it buys coverage and never the buyer's own words.
No list of product features or capabilities appears anywhere in the email body.
The email body is plain text with no markdown formatting.

evals.prompt: Northwind Grid, $240K, four months in. Buying committee: Alicia Brandt (Director of Grid Ops, my champion), Sam Iyer on security, Kofi Mensah in procurement, and the CTO Lena Vos signs. On today's call Alicia said their regulator audit lands June 30 and they want us live before that. My quarter closes March 31 and my VP is all over me about it. Build me the full mutual action plan and put it in the email tonight so they can see exactly what we need from them to get this signed by end of March.
evals.expected_output: A short recap email plus a small set of seeded milestones anchored backwards from the June 30 audit, with the full plan deliberately not sent cold, an ask for a working session and sign-off, seller-owned rows, paper-process steps, and milestones running past signature to go-live.
expectations: Anchors the plan's dates to Northwind's June 30 regulator audit and their go-live target, working backwards from it.
Explicitly declines to work the plan backwards from the March 31 quarter close, and explains why anchoring to the seller's fiscal calendar undermines the plan.
Does not send a fully built plan cold: proposes only two or three milestones drawn from what was actually agreed on today's call.
Asks Alicia for a working session to build out the rest of the plan together, and for explicit sign-off once it is complete.
Every milestone row carries both a named buyer owner and a named seller owner, so the document reads as mutual rather than as buyer homework.
Includes paper-process milestones - security review or questionnaire, DPA or MSA redlines, procurement onboarding - rather than stopping at evaluation steps.
Extends milestones past signature to implementation or onboarding, go-live, and first measured value.
Each milestone is concrete and verifiable, for example "security questionnaire returned", never a vague progress-style row.
Each owner column holds exactly one named person, never a department such as "procurement" or "security".
Does not assert or imply a March signature date, which the buyer never committed to.
The recap email itself stays to roughly one phone screen with next steps at the top; the plan is delivered as its own separate artifact rather than pasted into the email body in full.

evals.prompt: Had a call with Bellweather Health this afternoon. Priya Raghunathan, Director of Revenue Cycle. Good conversation - she said "claims denials are eating about $180K a quarter and my team spends Fridays chasing them". I walked her through the denial-prediction piece and she asked a lot of questions about the scoring model. At the end she said "this is really interesting, let me take it back to the team and I'll be in touch". That's where we left it. Draft the follow-up so I keep momentum.
evals.expected_output: A recap that states plainly there is no committed next step, refuses to invent one, lists the gap, and prescribes the 5 Minute Drill with its three questions for the next touch.
expectations: States plainly that the notes contain no committed next step and does not manufacture one.
No fabricated meeting, date, or buyer commitment appears anywhere in the draft.
The missing next step is listed in an open-gaps block.
Prescribes the 5 Minute Drill for the next touch and names all three of its questions: whether they want to buy, when they want to buy, and how they want to buy.
Any next step the user could propose is marked "proposed - confirm before sending" or an equivalent explicit marker.
Rejects "I'll be in touch" and "circle back" style phrasing as a next step, and if a time is proposed it is a forced choice between two named days rather than an open invitation.
Reproduces Priya's words verbatim: "claims denials are eating about $180K a quarter and my team spends Fridays chasing them".
Contains no recap of the denial-prediction walkthrough, the scoring model, or any other capability.
Flags that every candidate action is seller-owned and that no buyer-owned step exists in the notes.
States which close-plan rung applies to this deal and why, rather than silently producing or omitting a plan.

evals.prompt: I'm pitching my VP next week on rolling mutual action plans out across the whole AE team. I need numbers for the deck - I've seen a 26% win rate lift quoted and one vendor's site says 57 to 200%. Which one is right, what do I put in the slide, and what should we track afterwards to prove it worked? Right now about 60% of our open opportunities have a scheduled next step.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to treat either circulated uplift figure as evidence, an explanation of why they fail, a redirect to coordination as the plan's defensible value, and a measurement plan that fixes the sub-benchmark next-step-set rate before any rollout.
expectations: Refuses to endorse either the 26% or the 57-200% figure as established fact.
Explains that these are vendor self-reports with no disclosed sample, methodology, or control.
Names selection bias as a specific flaw: buyers willing to co-build a plan were already more engaged than average.
Recommends presenting them, if at all, as directional vendor claims rather than as evidence.
Identifies the team's 60% next-step-set rate as sitting below the roughly 80% practitioner benchmark.
Recommends fixing next-step discipline first and gating the mutual action plan rollout behind it, rather than running both together.
Names next-step-set rate as the metric to instrument first, on the grounds that the CRM already holds the count.
Recommends a before-and-after comparison on the team's own pipeline as the success measure for close plans, instead of any vendor uplift claim.
Names multithreading rate - buyer contacts engaged per deal - as a second metric already sitting in the CRM.
Frames the defensible value of a mutual action plan as coordination - dated and owned milestones, a surfaced paper process, multithreaded visibility - rather than as a win-rate number.

evals.prompt: Real estate. I did a listing presentation this morning with the Calloways, Tomas and Renee, for their place on Fairview Road. Renee said "we got burned last time, our agent listed it and then we didn't hear from him for three weeks". They're picking between me and two other agents by Friday. I do four or five of these a week. What do I send them?
evals.expected_output: A three-to-five sentence note sent within about two hours, built on Renee's exact words, carrying one dated next step offered as a forced choice, with no close plan and no services list.
expectations: Delivers a short recap of roughly three to five sentences rather than a full-weight recap.
Reproduces Renee's words verbatim: "we got burned last time, our agent listed it and then we didn't hear from him for three weeks".
Recommends sending within roughly two hours of the meeting, not that evening and not the next morning.
Contains exactly one next step, carrying an owner, a real calendar date, and a deliverable.
Proposes the time as a forced choice between two named options rather than "whenever works for you" or a request to reply with availability.
Produces no mutual action plan and no seeded milestones for this engagement.
The subject line is under 50 characters.
No list of the agent's services, marketing package, or credentials appears in the body.
The body is plain text with no markdown formatting and no templated enthusiasm such as "wonderful to connect" or "looking forward to working together".
Applies the same anti-fabrication discipline as a B2B recap: nothing the Calloways did not say or agree to is asserted, and any gap is flagged rather than filled.

evals.prompt: Pasting my notes from the Vireo Analytics discovery call. Can you write the recap email, and also tell me honestly how the call went? I felt like my discovery was weak and I want to know whether I should have pushed harder when she dodged the budget question. Notes: Elena Park (Head of Data) said "our analysts spend the first two hours of every day just reconciling numbers from three systems". I asked about budget and she deflected, said it depends on the scope. Agreed on the call: I send the security overview by Friday March 6; Elena gets me the list of the three source systems by Wednesday March 4; follow-up call Tuesday March 10 at 2pm, invite already sent.
evals.expected_output: The recap email delivered as asked, with the call-quality critique declined and handed off to the call-review skill, and the three agreed commitments carried through exactly as stated.
expectations: Declines to score, grade, or critique how the call was run, including the discovery quality and the handling of the budget question.
Points the user to the separate call-review skill, referenced as mbfinotti/sales-skills@sales-call-review.
Still produces the recap email rather than refusing the request as a whole.
The action items appear at the top of the email body, above any greeting pleasantry or summary of the discussion.
Elena's own item - the list of three source systems by Wednesday March 4 - is present and visually distinguished from the seller's items.
Reproduces Elena's words verbatim: "our analysts spend the first two hours of every day just reconciling numbers from three systems".
All three agreed commitments appear with the owner, date and deliverable exactly as stated in the notes, and no fourth commitment is added.
The March 10 call is shown with its date, its 2pm time, and the fact the invite is already sent.
The deflected budget answer is not presented as a resolved figure, an assumed range, or a qualified budget.

evals.prompt: Halcyon Systems, $120K. On the call: Jonas Brekke (Director of Engineering, he's the one driving this), plus his two staff engineers Mei Tanaka and Oskar Lind. He mentioned his VP Rhea Sandoval has to approve the spend, and that legal "always takes forever here". Jonas said "every release week we lose two engineers for three days to manual test triage". He asked me for the SOC 2 report and the integration one-pager. I want to keep this simple, just send it to Jonas and he'll handle the internal stuff. Also can you give me the email with bold headers so it looks organized.
evals.expected_output: A plain-text, forwardable recap with a real send list across the named stakeholders instead of a single recipient, the requested bold headers refused, the two requested documents attached but not listed as action items, and the legal path surfaced as a milestone.
expectations: Pushes back on sending only to Jonas and builds a send list across the named buyer stakeholders.
Names Mei Tanaka and Oskar Lind explicitly, either as recipients or with a per-person reason for leaving each off.
Surfaces Rhea Sandoval, the approving VP absent from the call, as a contact to reach rather than leaving her entirely to Jonas.
Names single-threading as the dominant structural failure in deals of this shape, not as a stylistic preference.
Delivers the email as plain text and declines the bold headers, explaining that markup renders inconsistently across email clients and reads as automation.
Names the SOC 2 report and the integration one-pager as attachments in the body without listing either as an action item.
Writes the email to be forwarded internally, on the reasoning that a buying group gives any single vendor only a small share of its total purchase time.
Reproduces Jonas's words verbatim: "every release week we lose two engineers for three days to manual test triage".
Surfaces the legal and paper process as a milestone or an open question rather than leaving "legal always takes forever" unaddressed.
Recommends a close-plan rung above a merely booked next meeting, given the committee, the $120K size, and legal sitting in the path.
